screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we focus on how to keep an SD‑WAN fabric observable and resilient. You will learn to use vManage as a single pane of glass for network health, device status, application performance, alarms, and audit trails. You will also learn the essential CLI commands on vEdge and cEdge routers to verify control plane peering, TLOC and IPsec tunnels, and local routing. Together these skills let you rapidly narrow faults from high‑level alarms to specific underlay or overlay causes. For example, vManage may show an alarm for a tunnel down; the CLI helps you confirm whether the problem is an IPsec SA or an underlay routing issue. We emphasize safe operational practices: start with show commands, avoid disruptive clears in production, and collect logs for support. By the end of this lesson you will have a repeatable troubleshooting flow and practical knowledge of day‑two tasks such as upgrades and backups. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like over‑reliance on dashboards or ignoring the underlay, and practice the diagnostic steps described in the hands‑on activity to build confidence.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › SD-WAN Monitoring
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

SD-WAN Monitoring, Troubleshooting, and Operations

Realize how centralized monitoring and device CLI work together to detect alarms, validate control and data planes, and perform safe day‑2 operations on an SD‑WAN fabric.

Key Tools
vManage dashboards • vEdge / cEdge CLI • Alarms & logs
Visual: cards show device status, application SLA, and a topology tile to emphasize central visibility.
In this lesson

Learn to read vManage dashboards, run show commands for control and data planes, and perform safe upgrades and backups.

Coming up

Troubleshooting flow, CLI examples, common mistakes, and a hands‑on connectivity lab scenario.

Outcome

Be able to triage alerts, confirm control and data plane health, and manage day‑2 tasks with confidence.

Explore Key Topics
vManage Monitoring
Dashboards for health, apps, and alarms.
CLI Verification
Show commands for control and data plane checks.
Day‑2 Operations
Upgrades, backups, templates and alerts.
Topology Snapshot
Site tiles: branch, data center, controllers. Status badges show if TLOCs are up and whether alarms exist. This reinforces the idea that topology and alarms are the first signals to inspect.
Quick tip
Always gather non‑disruptive state with show commands before making changes. That preserves evidence for later analysis.
Key Takeaway

Use vManage to detect and scope issues, then use CLI to verify and resolve control or data plane problems safely.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives map the practical abilities you'll develop. First, you'll learn to utilize vManage for comprehensive monitoring so you can quickly assess fabric health, spot alarms, and review application performance. Second, you'll interpret alarms, events, and audit logs to identify who made changes, when, and why, which is essential for responsible troubleshooting and compliance. Third, you'll apply essential CLI troubleshooting commands on vEdge and cEdge routers to validate control plane peering and data plane tunnel status; knowing which show command to run speeds root cause analysis. Finally, you'll understand day‑two operations like software upgrades and backup and restore procedures so you can maintain availability and recover from failures. Each objective is grounded in everyday operational needs: reducing downtime, proving whether a problem is overlay versus underlay, and ensuring safe changes. By practicing these skills in the hands‑on activity you will move from theory to a repeatable workflow that makes operations predictable and auditable.

screens.title: vManage Monitoring — Dashboards and Topology
screens.narratorSegment: vManage is the centralized monitoring tool for the SD‑WAN fabric. It gives you a high‑level Network dashboard that summarizes fabric health and connected devices, a Devices dashboard that lists each vEdge, cEdge, vSmart and vBond with uptime and resource usage, and a Topology view that maps sites and TLOC tunnel states. Learning to read these dashboards is the first step in a troubleshooting flow: alarms often show up here before users file tickets. For example, a Network alarm that a tunnel is down should push you to view the device's interface and tunnel statistics and then check related events in the Alarms and Events log. Notice how vManage provides application performance metrics like loss, latency and jitter across transports; that helps you validate whether AAR policies are steering traffic appropriately. A common misconception is treating vManage as a cure‑all. vManage surfaces symptoms and historical evidence, but it may not reveal underlay routing or firewall blocks. Always collect vManage alarms, note timestamps and then move to targeted CLI checks. Practice reading the topology and Device details so you can form a hypothesis before making changes. Ask yourself: does the alarm indicate overlay failure, or could the underlay be the root cause?

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › vManage Monitoring
Definition

vManage dashboards and topology

vManage aggregates health, device metrics, topology and application performance so you can spot and prioritize issues across the fabric.

Network Dashboard
Fabric health summary, connected device count, and active alarms to begin triage.
Device Details
Per device CPU, memory, interfaces, tunnel states and local logs for targeted diagnosis.
Topology View
Graphical layout of sites and tunnels to identify broken or degraded paths visually.
Scenario & Example
Example: an alarm shows a TLOC down. The correct flow is to record the alarm timestamp, open the device details for both ends of the tunnel, and check interface and IPsec statistics. If vManage shows packet loss for an application, confirm which transport carried the traffic and whether AAR policies are configured and active.
Checklist
  • Note alarm and event timestamps.
  • Open Device details for interface and tunnel stats.
  • Correlate with application performance tiles.
Common mistake
Assuming vManage alarm equals overlay failure. Always confirm underlay reachability and firewall state before changing overlay settings.
Key Takeaway

Use vManage to scope issues and gather evidence, then use CLI to confirm whether the underlay or overlay is at fault.

screens.title: Device Status and Topology Details
screens.narratorSegment: Device status in vManage and on the router gives an immediate sense of health. Device tiles show uptime, C P U and memory utilization, interface states, and per‑device logs. These details let you separate resource issues from connectivity issues. For example, high C P U or memory may explain intermittent control plane drops, so verifying system health with the show sdwan system status command is important before changing network configuration. The topology view maps TLOCs and their colors so you can identify which transport is being used by each site. TLOC attributes such as color and encapsulation must match peers for tunnels to form correctly. A frequent misconception is to assume any tunnel failure is a policy issue; often it’s a mismatched TLOC color, encapsulation mismatch, or an underlay firewall blocking UDP ports. Use a quick sequence: confirm the device is up in vManage, check C P U and memory, inspect interface states with show interface, and validate TLOCs with show sdwan omp tlocs. That sequence prevents wasted effort and points to the right troubleshooting domain. Device Status and Topology Details means device resource and tloc details narrow the fault domain: resource, underlay, or overlay.. In practical terms, what device metrics reveal about availability and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Device Status & Topology
Architecture

Device metrics and topology details

Use per device metrics to detect resource constraints and the topology map to trace TLOC relationships and transport colors.

Key Device Metrics
Uptime, CPU, memory, interface errors, tunnel uptime and local logs provide the context for performance symptoms.
Topology and TLOCs
Topology shows which TLOCs connect sites and which transport colors are active. TLOC attributes explain tunnel negotiation behavior.
Practical steps
  1. Confirm device reachability in vManage.
  2. Run show sdwan system status to check CPU and memory.
  3. Inspect interfaces with show interface to find errors or down states.
  4. Validate TLOCs with show sdwan omp tlocs on the edge device.
Common mistake
Ignoring device resource exhaustion. High CPU can cause control plane instability even when links are up.
Pro tip
Compare TLOC colors and encapsulation between peers before assuming policy or route issues.
Key Takeaway

Device metrics and topology details should always shape your next CLI checks; they reveal whether the problem is resource, underlay, or overlay related.

screens.title: Application Performance and AAR Visibility
screens.narratorSegment: Application performance monitoring in vManage is a central strength of SD‑WAN. vManage reports latency, packet loss and jitter per application across available transports. This allows you to validate whether Application‑Aware Routing policies are steering traffic as intended. Start by identifying the affected application in the Applications dashboard and note which transport it is currently using. If the application shows SLA violations but the policy should prefer MPLS, check whether the MPLS path meets the SLA thresholds or if the application is being misidentified by the match conditions. On the router, use the show sdwan app-route stats command to view real‑time path quality and confirm what paths are being used. A common misconception is to blame policy immediately; often the overlay steers away because a transport is failing to meet SLA metrics. To diagnose, compare vManage application metrics with the device app-route stats and the OMP/TLOC routes. That comparison tells you whether to fix a transport, adjust SLA thresholds, or correct the application match rule. The goal is to align observed metrics, policy intent, and device behavior into one coherent picture.

keyIdea.title: Align metrics, policy, and device state
keyIdea.text: Compare vManage application metrics with device app-route stats to confirm AAR decisions and root cause.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Application Performance
Comparison

vManage metrics vs router app stats

vManage shows application performance centrally; router app stats show the actual path choices and live quality used for steering.

What to compare
  • vManage latency, loss, jitter per transport
  • Device app-route stats showing chosen path and quality
  • AAR policy SLA thresholds and match conditions
Example
If vManage shows high latency on MPLS and the router's app-route stats also mark MPLS as failing SLA, AAR will steer traffic to the alternate transport. The correct fix may be to resolve the MPLS underlay or adjust SLA thresholds if they are too strict for the link’s normal behavior.
Checklist
Confirm app identity, check vManage metrics, run show sdwan app-route stats, and validate AAR policy from vSmart.
Misconception
AAR not steering does not always mean policy error. It can mean the preferred transport is not meeting SLA thresholds.
Key Takeaway

Validate AAR by aligning vManage metrics, router path stats, and the intended policy to decide whether policy change or transport repair is required.

screens.title: Control Plane Verification — Essential show commands
screens.narratorSegment: Verifying the control plane is a predictable set of checks. Start with show sdwan control connections to confirm DTLS or TLS connections to vSmart and vBond and to see their state and endpoints. Next run show sdwan omp peers to check OMP peering state; look for the STATE column to read up or down and note the SITE ID and domain. Use show sdwan omp routes to inspect vRoutes learned and advertised; that tells you whether prefixes are present. Finally, show sdwan omp tlocs reveals local and remote TLOC information and helps you confirm the available transports and their attributes. A useful sequence is: confirm connectivity to controller IPs, verify OMP peers are up, confirm the prefix is present in the OMP routes, and then look at TLOCs to ensure the correct transport is available. A common misconception is to treat a single failed peer as catastrophic; redundant controllers and peering paths often provide resilience. However, if multiple peers show the same problem, focus on underlay connectivity and certificate validity. These commands provide the control plane picture you need to decide next steps.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Control Plane Verification
Code Walkthrough

Essential show commands

Use these commands to validate controller connections, OMP peering, routes, and TLOCs as the first control plane checks.

show sdwan control connections
show sdwan omp peers
show sdwan omp routes
show sdwan omp tlocs
Run these non‑disruptive show commands to gather control plane state before taking any action.
Practical checks and meaning
  • Check control connections state and endpoint IPs to confirm reachability.
  • Use OMP peers to verify peering state and uptime to vSmart.
  • Look at OMP routes to ensure the prefix you expect is present and learned.
  • Validate TLOCs to see which transports and colors are available for the device.
Common mistake
Skipping controller IP reachability checks. If the underlay cannot reach controller addresses, OMP will not form even when device looks healthy locally.
Key Takeaway

Control plane show commands give you the authoritative view of whether devices are exchanging routing information and which TLOCs are present.

screens.title: Data Plane Verification — IPsec and Tunnel Checks
screens.narratorSegment: Data plane failures require focused verification of IPsec sessions and tunnel interfaces. The primary commands are show sdwan ipsec connections to confirm the status of IPsec tunnels between TLOCs, and show crypto ipsec sa or show crypto ikev2 sa to inspect detailed security association states. Use show sdwan interface tunnel to verify tunnel interface statistics and packet counters. For end‑to‑end reachability, use ping vpn with a source and vpn id and traceroute vpn likewise. If a tunnel is down, check underlay reachability between TLOC IPs with a basic ping; firewalls often block required UDP ports such as 500, 4500 or the DTLS/TLS port used for control connections. A common pitfall is to clear or reset tunnels in production before documenting their state; always collect show outputs and consider a staged repair. When multiple redundant tunnels exist, note which tunnel is down and whether traffic is failing over to another transport. That informs whether service is degraded or fully down and helps prioritize remediation. Data Plane Verification — IPsec and Tunnel Checks means use ipsec and tunnel interface commands plus vpn ping/traceroute to diagnose data plane issues before any disruptive action.. In practical terms, commands to validate ipsec sas, tunnel interfaces, and path reachability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Data Plane Verification
Code Walkthrough

IPsec and tunnel commands

These commands verify IPsec SAs, IKEv2 state and tunnel interface statistics, and support path tests using vpn ping and traceroute.

show sdwan ipsec connections
show crypto ipsec sa
show crypto ikev2 sa
show sdwan interface tunnel
ping vpn <vpn-id> <destination-ip> source <source-ip>
traceroute vpn <vpn-id> <destination-ip> source <source-ip>
Troubleshooting tips
  • Verify underlay reachability between TLOC IPs first.
  • Check firewall/ACLs for blocked UDP ports required for IPsec and control plane.
  • When SAs are down, collect logs and do not clear unless you have maintenance windows.
Scenario
If show sdwan ipsec connections shows a tunnel down to one TLOC IP but another transport is up, the traffic may be successfully failing over. Focus on restoring the down tunnel and confirming underlay reachability to that TLOC.
Key Takeaway

Data plane checks confirm whether traffic paths are available and whether failover is occurring. Always validate underlay reachability first.

screens.title: General Device Health and Logging
screens.narratorSegment: Device health checks and logs provide important context for intermittent or systemic issues. Run show sdwan system status for an overall view of C P U, memory, and system uptime. Use show interface to inspect physical interface statistics, errors, and drops which can point to duplex, speed or hardware problems. For logs, show logging on the device collects recent syslog messages and warnings that may correlate with alarms seen in vManage. If you observe repeated warnings such as frequent IKE rekeys or repeated authentication failures, collect the logs and timestamps for correlation with vManage events. A common misconception is that logs are only useful after a failure; in reality, baseline logging during healthy periods helps you compare and spot anomalies. Keep in mind that show commands are non‑disruptive and should be your first actions. When you need vendor support, a troubleshooting data report from vManage combined with device show outputs gives support the evidence they need to analyze systemic issues. In practical terms, show commands and logging to find warnings and errors on devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Device Health & Logging
Definition

System status, interfaces and logs

Gather system status and logs as non‑disruptive evidence to trace intermittent failures and resource exhaustion.

Useful commands
show sdwan system status
show interface <interface-name>
show logging
Practical guidance
  • Collect system status and interface counters before making changes.
  • Keep log timestamps to correlate with vManage alarms and events.
  • Use logs to detect recurring conditions like rekeys or authentication errors.
Pro tip
Establish a baseline of healthy system metrics and logs so you can spot deviations quickly during incidents.
Key Takeaway

Collect show outputs and logs as first‑class evidence. This preserves the timeline and helps support teams reproduce issues.

screens.title: Common Troubleshooting Scenarios

Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Troubleshooting Flow
Process

Systematic troubleshooting steps

Use a repeatable sequence so you can quickly isolate whether an issue is overlay, underlay, or resource related.

1. Observe
Check Network dashboard, Topology, and Alarms and Events for symptoms and timestamps.
2. Scope
Open device details for affected sites and note resource and interface state.
3. Decide
Run control plane shows or data plane shows to decide the fault domain.
4. Verify
Collect show outputs and logs, and compare with vManage evidence before changes.
5. Resolve
Apply targeted fixes, test, and monitor. Use staged rollbacks where possible.
6. Document
Record what you observed, commands run, and the final resolution for future reference.
Common mistakes
Jumping to clears or configuration changes without collecting evidence; ignoring underlay reachability or firewall rules.
Key Takeaway

A consistent flow — observe, scope, decide, verify, resolve, document — reduces mistakes and speeds recovery.

screens.title: Lab Walkthrough: Troubleshoot Branch to Data Center Connectivity
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk a concrete scenario: a user at Branch Site 10 cannot reach a data center server at 172.16.20.10. The first safe CLI step is to verify local VPN reachability with a vpn ping to the branch gateway; this confirms local host stack is fine. Next, verify OMP peering with show sdwan omp peers to confirm the branch has established control plane relationships with vSmart. Then check show sdwan omp routes filtering for the destination prefix to ensure the branch has learned the route. After that, validate IPsec tunnels with show sdwan ipsec connections and inspect whether the TLOC to the data center is up or down. If a tunnel is down, run show crypto ipsec sa and show crypto ikev2 sa to inspect SA details. The chapter provides an example output where OMP peers are up and routes for 172.16.20.0/24 exist, but one IPsec tunnel to 10.0.2.1 is down while another is up. The ping still succeeds because traffic fails over to the available transport. That tells you the issue is a single transport failure, not total connectivity loss. The right next step is to investigate the underlay to the downed TLOC, check firewall ports and encapsulation, and coordinate with the remote site to restore the failed tunnel.

Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Lab Walkthrough
Scenario

Branch Site 10 cannot reach 172.16.20.10

Follow a safe, ordered sequence of non‑disruptive CLI checks to identify whether the problem is underlay, control plane, or data plane.

Step sequence
  1. Ping local VPN gateway to verify host reachability.
  2. show sdwan omp peers to confirm OMP peering.
  3. show sdwan omp routes | include 172.16.20.0/24 to check learned routes.
  4. show sdwan ipsec connections | include <dc TLOC IP> to inspect tunnels.
  5. ping vpn <vpn-id> 172.16.20.10 source <source-ip> for end‑to‑end test.
Branch1# show sdwan omp peers ... vsmart ... STATE up ... Branch1# show sdwan omp routes | include 172.16.20.0/24 ... 172.16.20.0/24 10.0.2.1 mpls ipsec R ... Branch1# show sdwan ipsec connections | include 10.0.2.1 ... 10.0.2.1 ... STATE down ... Branch1# ping vpn 10 172.16.20.10 source 192.168.10.5 !!!!! Success rate 100% ...
Interpretation: route exists and ping succeeds, but one IPsec SA is down. Traffic is using an alternate transport.
Diagnosis
A downed IPsec SA with successful ping indicates redundancy is working and the issue is a single transport failure. Investigate underlay reachability, firewall rules and the remote cEdge TLOC for the downed transport.
Next steps
  • Ping the downed TLOC IP to test underlay.
  • Check firewall logs for blocked UDP 500/4500 or ports used for DTLS/TLS.
  • Coordinate with the DC site to check their TLOC and interfaces.
Key Takeaway

Combine vManage evidence with device show outputs to identify whether an outage is a full failure or a single transport degradation with failover in place.

screens.title: Software Upgrades, Backup and Restore, and Templates
screens.narratorSegment: Day‑two operations keep your fabric healthy over time. For software upgrades, vManage lets you stage images, push them to devices and perform controlled activations with rollback options. Always follow documented upgrade paths and test in a lab before production. For backups, schedule regular vManage configuration backups and retain device configuration exports; these are your recovery artifacts in case of controller failure. Template management in vManage provides consistent configurations across many devices; use templates to apply changes at scale and reduce configuration drift. Monitoring and alerting should be configured to send email, SNMP or syslog for critical alarms so teams respond proactively. A common mistake is performing upgrades without a tested rollback or without collecting a pre‑upgrade backup of the vManage and device configurations. Another pitfall is changing templates in production without a staged validation. Always maintain a maintenance window, document changes, and verify post‑upgrade device states. These practices make operations predictable and reduce prolonged outages. Module 4 › Chapter 3.7 › Day‑2 Operations
Process

Upgrades, backups and template management

Plan upgrades, back up configurations, and use templates to keep devices consistent and recoverable.

Software Upgrades
Stage images in vManage, test in a lab, push in controlled batches, and use rollback when available.
Backup & Restore
Schedule vManage backups and export device configs to ensure recoverability of controller and device state.
Template Management
Use templates to apply consistent settings across devices and reduce manual errors during changes.
Monitoring & Alerting
Configure alerts to email, SNMP or syslog for timely operational response to critical events.
Operational checklist
  • Collect backups before upgrades.
  • Test upgrades in lab and stage to limited sites first.
  • Document rollback and maintenance windows.
Common mistake
Performing upgrades without a recent backup or without verifying template application results in prolonged recovery time if issues occur.
Key Takeaway

Plan upgrades and backups, use templates for consistency, and configure alerts to enable proactive operations and quick recovery.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Safe Troubleshooting Practices
screens.narratorSegment: Safety and discipline are as important as technical skill when troubleshooting production SD‑WAN. Always begin with non‑disruptive show commands to collect evidence. Avoid clearing control plane or data plane sessions during initial investigation unless you have a maintenance window and rollback plan. Document timestamps, alarms, and command outputs to create a clear timeline for later analysis. Be cautious about over‑reliance on vManage — it is invaluable for visibility, but the CLI reveals low‑level details such as IPsec SA state and local interface errors. Don’t ignore the underlay: many overlay problems have underlay root causes such as routing or firewall issues. Establish baselines of normal performance so you can recognize deviations quickly. Finally, treat template and upgrade changes as high‑risk actions — stage images and template updates, test them in lab, and schedule predictable maintenance windows. Following these practices reduces incident duration and helps maintain service continuity while you investigate and remediate. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we focus on how to keep an SD‑WAN fabric observable and resilient. You will learn to use vManage as a single pane of glass for network health, device status, application performance, alarms, and audit trails. You will also learn the essential CLI commands on vEdge and cEdge routers to verify control plane peering, TLOC and IPsec tunnels, and local routing. Together these skills let you rapidly narrow faults from high‑level alarms to specific underlay or overlay causes. For example, vManage may show an alarm for a tunnel down; the CLI helps you confirm whether the problem is an IPsec SA or an underlay routing issue. We emphasize safe operational practices: start with show commands, avoid disruptive clears in production, and collect logs for support. By the end of this lesson you will have a repeatable troubleshooting flow and practical knowledge of day‑two tasks such as upgrades and backups. Keep an eye out for common mistakes like over‑reliance on dashboards or ignoring the underlay, and practice the diagnostic steps described in the hands‑on activity to build confidence.

These objectives map the practical abilities you'll develop. First, you'll learn to utilize vManage for comprehensive monitoring so you can quickly assess fabric health, spot alarms, and review application performance. Second, you'll interpret alarms, events, and audit logs to identify who made changes, when, and why, which is essential for responsible troubleshooting and compliance. Third, you'll apply essential CLI troubleshooting commands on vEdge and cEdge routers to validate control plane peering and data plane tunnel status; knowing which show command to run speeds root cause analysis. Finally, you'll understand day‑two operations like software upgrades and backup and restore procedures so you can maintain availability and recover from failures. Each objective is grounded in everyday operational needs: reducing downtime, proving whether a problem is overlay versus underlay, and ensuring safe changes. By practicing these skills in the hands‑on activity you will move from theory to a repeatable workflow that makes operations predictable and auditable.

This second objectives screen focuses on the applied tasks that you will practice. First, monitor network health and topology to understand device connectivity and tunnel status; this helps you detect when a site becomes isolated or when a TLOC is down. Second, diagnose control plane versus data plane failures so you know whether to inspect OMP peering or IPsec tunnels. Third, use application performance metrics and Application‑Aware Routing visibility to confirm whether AAR is steering traffic correctly and to identify SLA violations. Fourth, manage templates, backups, and alerting so site configurations remain consistent and recoverable. Each objective translates into concrete actions: open the Network dashboard, examine alarms and events, run specific show commands, and keep a scheduled backup. Practicing this sequence makes operations predictable and reduces risk when you perform upgrades or policy changes.

vManage is the centralized monitoring tool for the SD‑WAN fabric. It gives you a high‑level Network dashboard that summarizes fabric health and connected devices, a Devices dashboard that lists each vEdge, cEdge, vSmart and vBond with uptime and resource usage, and a Topology view that maps sites and TLOC tunnel states. Learning to read these dashboards is the first step in a troubleshooting flow: alarms often show up here before users file tickets. For example, a Network alarm that a tunnel is down should push you to view the device's interface and tunnel statistics and then check related events in the Alarms and Events log. Notice how vManage provides application performance metrics like loss, latency and jitter across transports; that helps you validate whether AAR policies are steering traffic appropriately. A common misconception is treating vManage as a cure‑all. vManage surfaces symptoms and historical evidence, but it may not reveal underlay routing or firewall blocks. Always collect vManage alarms, note timestamps and then move to targeted CLI checks. Practice reading the topology and Device details so you can form a hypothesis before making changes. Ask yourself: does the alarm indicate overlay failure, or could the underlay be the root cause?

Device status in vManage and on the router gives an immediate sense of health. Device tiles show uptime, C P U and memory utilization, interface states, and per‑device logs. These details let you separate resource issues from connectivity issues. For example, high C P U or memory may explain intermittent control plane drops, so verifying system health with the show sdwan system status command is important before changing network configuration. The topology view maps TLOCs and their colors so you can identify which transport is being used by each site. TLOC attributes such as color and encapsulation must match peers for tunnels to form correctly. A frequent misconception is to assume any tunnel failure is a policy issue; often it’s a mismatched TLOC color, encapsulation mismatch, or an underlay firewall blocking UDP ports. Use a quick sequence: confirm the device is up in vManage, check C P U and memory, inspect interface states with show interface, and validate TLOCs with show sdwan omp tlocs. That sequence prevents wasted effort and points to the right troubleshooting domain. Device Status and Topology Details means device resource and tloc details narrow the fault domain: resource, underlay, or overlay.. In practical terms, what device metrics reveal about availability and performance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Application performance monitoring in vManage is a central strength of SD‑WAN. vManage reports latency, packet loss and jitter per application across available transports. This allows you to validate whether Application‑Aware Routing policies are steering traffic as intended. Start by identifying the affected application in the Applications dashboard and note which transport it is currently using. If the application shows SLA violations but the policy should prefer MPLS, check whether the MPLS path meets the SLA thresholds or if the application is being misidentified by the match conditions. On the router, use the show sdwan app-route stats command to view real‑time path quality and confirm what paths are being used. A common misconception is to blame policy immediately; often the overlay steers away because a transport is failing to meet SLA metrics. To diagnose, compare vManage application metrics with the device app-route stats and the OMP/TLOC routes. That comparison tells you whether to fix a transport, adjust SLA thresholds, or correct the application match rule. The goal is to align observed metrics, policy intent, and device behavior into one coherent picture.

Verifying the control plane is a predictable set of checks. Start with show sdwan control connections to confirm DTLS or TLS connections to vSmart and vBond and to see their state and endpoints. Next run show sdwan omp peers to check OMP peering state; look for the STATE column to read up or down and note the SITE ID and domain. Use show sdwan omp routes to inspect vRoutes learned and advertised; that tells you whether prefixes are present. Finally, show sdwan omp tlocs reveals local and remote TLOC information and helps you confirm the available transports and their attributes. A useful sequence is: confirm connectivity to controller IPs, verify OMP peers are up, confirm the prefix is present in the OMP routes, and then look at TLOCs to ensure the correct transport is available. A common misconception is to treat a single failed peer as catastrophic; redundant controllers and peering paths often provide resilience. However, if multiple peers show the same problem, focus on underlay connectivity and certificate validity. These commands provide the control plane picture you need to decide next steps.

Data plane failures require focused verification of IPsec sessions and tunnel interfaces. The primary commands are show sdwan ipsec connections to confirm the status of IPsec tunnels between TLOCs, and show crypto ipsec sa or show crypto ikev2 sa to inspect detailed security association states. Use show sdwan interface tunnel to verify tunnel interface statistics and packet counters. For end‑to‑end reachability, use ping vpn with a source and vpn id and traceroute vpn likewise. If a tunnel is down, check underlay reachability between TLOC IPs with a basic ping; firewalls often block required UDP ports such as 500, 4500 or the DTLS/TLS port used for control connections. A common pitfall is to clear or reset tunnels in production before documenting their state; always collect show outputs and consider a staged repair. When multiple redundant tunnels exist, note which tunnel is down and whether traffic is failing over to another transport. That informs whether service is degraded or fully down and helps prioritize remediation. Data Plane Verification — IPsec and Tunnel Checks means use ipsec and tunnel interface commands plus vpn ping/traceroute to diagnose data plane issues before any disruptive action.. In practical terms, commands to validate ipsec sas, tunnel interfaces, and path reachability. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Device health checks and logs provide important context for intermittent or systemic issues. Run show sdwan system status for an overall view of C P U, memory, and system uptime. Use show interface to inspect physical interface statistics, errors, and drops which can point to duplex, speed or hardware problems. For logs, show logging on the device collects recent syslog messages and warnings that may correlate with alarms seen in vManage. If you observe repeated warnings such as frequent IKE rekeys or repeated authentication failures, collect the logs and timestamps for correlation with vManage events. A common misconception is that logs are only useful after a failure; in reality, baseline logging during healthy periods helps you compare and spot anomalies. Keep in mind that show commands are non‑disruptive and should be your first actions. When you need vendor support, a troubleshooting data report from vManage combined with device show outputs gives support the evidence they need to analyze systemic issues. General Device Health and Logging means system and interface logs, combined with show outputs, create the timeline you need to correlate events and root cause.. In practical terms, show commands and logging to find warnings and errors on devices. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

A repeatable troubleshooting flow reduces guesswork during incidents. Start high with vManage: check the Network dashboard and the Alarms and Events list to identify symptoms and timestamps. Next, scope to devices: review device status and topology to find which sites or TLOCs are impacted. Then decide control or data plane by running the control plane commands show sdwan control connections and show sdwan omp peers versus data plane checks like show sdwan ipsec connections and show crypto ipsec sa.
